speechtext: Amidst a great many interruptions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO READJUST REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
-that the second amendment of 1949 was unwise. In other words he does challenge its wisdom. Apparently, though, he is not challenging its validity. I have not heard that there has been any appeal to the courts as to the validity of that statute. The fact of the matter is that it arose out of a joint resolution of both houses of the Canadian parliament, and that the enacting legislation was passed by the parliament at Westminster. It does seem to me clearly to be the law of the land.
The only question at issue here is whether or not redistribution is a federal matter. If it is, then I contend we have the right to deal with it in this parliament. Indeed, we have always had that right. On previous occasions we exercised in this parliament the right to deal with redistribution when we passed joint resolutions and asked Westminster to pass the necessary amendment to the British North America Act.
The only change now is that we are able to exercise that right by passing the amendment right here in this parliament. The hon. member for Eglinton does not like what he refers to as the reducing of the constitution to a mere bill. As a matter of fact it now requires more stages in this parliament to amend the British North America Act than it did formerly. Previously, all it took so far as Canada was concerned was a one stage resolution in this house and a one stage resolution in the Senate, and it did not even require

British North America Act
royal assent. Now it requires that a bill be put through all the stages in this house and all the stages of the Senate, and that it shall have royal assent. Actually, so far as Canada is concerned, we have made it a bit more difficult to amend the British North America Act. The only thing we have done away with is the perfunctory formality of going over to Westminster, and we supported that change very strongly.
What has been the history of amendments to the British North America Act with respect to redistribution? I must not spend too much time on this because, as a matter of fact, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) referred to the matter in his remarks this afternoon. In fact there have been four cases where amendments to the British North America Act were sought and obtained, which dealt precisely with representation in the House of Commons.
There was the amendment of 1886 which provided for the right to establish representation from territories or areas outside the organized provinces of this country. Dr. Olli-vier, in his book "British North America Acts and Selected Statutes," points out that when that amendment was obtained in 1886-and I quote from page 99 of his book-
The provinces were not consulted, and did not ask to be consulted, though if the British North America Act was a treaty, modification in the representation in parliament, changing the balance of sectional power, might have been contended to require the consent of the existing provinces.
The second of the four amendments to which I refer was the one in 1915 which, among other things, established the senatorial floor under the number of members the provinces should have in the House of Commons. That, too, was passed without consulting the provinces. Prince Edward Island made representations that there be such a floor, but no other provinces were consulted. I may point out that, even as the first of these two changes was in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald as prime minister of this country, the second was in the days of Sir Robert Borden. It seems those two Conservative prime ministers had no doubt about it. They accepted the fact that redistribution was a matter of concern to the federal parliament.
The other two occasions of the four to which I am now referring are within the memory of many, if not most, hon. members now in the house. There was the one in 1943, when redistribution was postponed by means of an amendment to the British North America Act, and the one in 1946 when the rules under section 51 were changed again by obtaining an amendment to the British North America Act.

On neither of those occasions were the provinces consulted. I have always been under the impression that lawyers were governed heavily by precedent. Yet here we have a lawyer today, the hon. member for Eglinton, a stare decisis lawyer at that, seemingly ignoring all these precedents and wanting us now to do it in another way.
This afternoon the hon. member had a great deal to say about the opposition of his party, not only to the amendment of 1949 that won the right for parliament to amend the constitution in federal matters, but also the opposition of his party to the amendment of 1946, when we changed the rules under section 51 of the British North America Act. But he seems to gloss over rather quickly the experience of 1943. That, too, was an occasion when we amended the British North America Act with respect to the matter covered in section 51. On that occasion we postponed redistribution because of the war situation.
I find that on that occasion the person who spoke for the Progressive Conservative party was the then leader of the official opposition, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). In his speech at that time he did not make a solitary reference to the idea that the provinces should be consulted, but simply gave the motion his support. He did get into an argument with the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) over some matters that were perhaps irrelevant to the issue before the house at that time. But, as recorded at page 4344 of Hansard, he gave the support of his party to that motion, without any question whatsoever. When one looks at the recorded vote on that occasion, as it is found at page 4367 of Hansard for July 5, 1943, we find there were only nine people in the House of Commons who registered their votes against that amendment. Those nine were all independent members from the province of Quebec who sat over here in the southeast corner. The 115 yeas included all the Progressive Conservative members who were in the house at that time. There is one case where they actually voted for an amendment to the British North America Act dealing with what is in section 51 without raising the question as to whether or not the provinces should be consulted. To complete the picture I should say that in that debate one Progressive Conservative member, Mr. King Hazen, did raise the point, but it was not raised officially by the spokesman for that party.
In addition to those four instances which dealt directly with the question of representation in this house, there were the others to which the minister referred, the case in

1871 and the case in 1916 when the life of parliament was extended, and the bill in 1949 which resulted in adding to this parliament seven members for Newfoundland.
I find the case of 1871 most interesting because of some footnotes which Dr. Ollivier has put in his book, to which I have already referred. He points out that in that instance the amendment was actually sought by the executive, by the cabinet, before the decision was made in parliament. Later the matter was the subject of discussion in parliament and parliament by a vote of 137 to 0 decided that no change in the provisions of the British North America Act should be sought by the executive of the government without the previous assent of parliament. That is the position that has been accepted and which has never since been contested. However, in the next paragraph in the footnote Dr. Ollivier states:
David Mills moved a resolution to the effect that any alteration in the principles of representation in the House of Commons without the consent of the several provinces to the original compact, would be a violation of the federal principle of the constitution, but the resolution was rejected without debate.
Mr. Mills was the member for Bothwell in that parliament. I submit that all the precedents are clear and that in the whole history of this country, so far as redistribution is concerned, it has been accepted that it is a federal matter and that whenever a change is indicated it is within the power of the federal parliament to seek that change. Previously we sought it by a joint resolution to Westminster; now the only change is that we have the right to make an amendment by a bill passed by this parliament.
Some attention, in fact, should be paid to the actual wording of section 51 of the British North America Act, which is quite clear and which states in part that on the completion of each decennial census the representation shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner and from, such time as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides. That is clear. The federal parliament is given the responsibility over redistribution. Indeed that is giving to the parliament of Canada the same authority over federal redistribution as section 92 gives to the provincial legislatures over redistribution within the provinces.
In my view the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has not answered the very pointed questions on that aspect of the matter which have been put to him from the other side. As I say, it seems to me that the position taken in the amendment now before us challenges the validity of section 91, subsection 1, as it was enacted by the second
British North America Act amendment to the British North America Act of 1949. It challenges all precedents in our history in respect to this matter. Furthermore, as I see it, it seems to me to do all the things which the hon. member for Eglinton claims that this bill does.
The hon. member seems to regard this bill as a threat to confederation, as a denial of all the principles of federal and constitutional government, but actually if we were to accept the position of his amendment that every time it is necessary to adjust the constitution even with respect to federal matters, we would have to go through the routine of consulting the provinces, which implies getting their consent, we are going to hog-tie our constitution and prevent the possibility of any change or progress in this country. Maybe the hon. member and his party want it that way; we do not.
I regard it as important that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton should be defeated so that we make it clear that we are not going to permit ourselves to become hog-tied in that way.
Surely it is part and parcel of the whole theory and practice of democratic government that we should not forever be tied to the past. What we may yet do in the way of sorting out the various means of amending our constitution in respect to matters provincial or matters that are of mutual concern is another question. I hope the day will come when we do get that problem sorted out and our entire constitution becomes a Canadian document. In the meantime let us not go back on such progress as we have made in respect to amending the constitution in federal matters.
It has been established across the years that this parliament is responsible for redistribution. It has now been established, even if my hon. friends to my right do not like it, that this parliament of Canada has the right to amend the constitution with respect to federal matters, of which redistribution is one. In my view it would be a mistake, it would be a retrograde step, it would be tying our hands for the future and holding Canada back if we took the position set out in the amendment of the hon. member for Eglinton.
I shall leave it at that. As I have already indicated, there is another phase of the matter which we feel should be dealt with, but in the nature of the case it will be necessary to wait until this amendment has been disposed of before we can bring the other matter we have in mind before the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO READJUST REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go over the arguments that were presented on an earlier occasion when this same subject matter was under discussion and when a vote was not taken in relation to the argument then put forward. It does seem to me, however, that there has been a very strange disregard of a position that had never been challenged in this house until comparatively recent years. Going back over the debates in the house on any occasion when this subject has been under consideration, the leading spokesman of both the Conservative and the Liberal parties have always taken the position that the British North America Act is a compact and that in those matters affecting the interests of the provinces changes should not be made which could affect their interests without the provinces having an opportunity to express their opinions and to discuss the subject matter raised.
I noticed that during the time the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) was speaking this afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) challenged him on more than one occasion with regard to the statement that there should be consultation with the provinces. The hon. member for Eglinton was asked if that meant consent. This question has been asked on other occasions and apparently implies the proposition that the government does not expect consent. Before a question of that kind is put forward as an implied answer to the suggestion that there should be consultation, perhaps it could be met by another question. If the government seriously contemplates some measure of success in the discussions it initiated with the provinces for the purpose of seeking a basis for amendment of the British North America Act, what does it suggest as the basis on which that agreed method of amendment is going to be arrived at? After all, this government now has the responsibility for producing any
[Mr. Fair.)

results that can be produced by it in dealing with the provinces. Do not ask the opposition at this point how they would deal with this matter as though that in itself was an answer to arguments put forward with respect to the necessity for consultation at a time when the government itself is consulting with the provinces presumably with the expectation that some satisfactory system may be worked out for the amendment of our own constitution.
Unless the government believe there is a possibility of arriving at common ground, then they have engaged in what they regard as a fruitless endeavour from the very outset. I hesitate to believe that they are parties to such a sham. I hesitate to believe that they invited the provinces to meet with them and discuss possible procedures of amendment of the British North America Act without some belief that there is a possibility of reaching common ground and a meeting of minds as to the manner in which the amendment of our constitution shall take place. Anything else would suggest such a cynical approach to this great question by the government as would be a challenge to the possibility of any satisfactory dealings between this government and the provinces at any time.
The Prime Minister, the minister who has moved the motion for second reading of the bill and other members who appear to be ready to support this procedure are well aware that men who were regarded for years as possessing a very great knowledge of our constitution, men like Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe and others, always insisted upon the proposition that there could be no question about the necessity for consulting the provinces if a new basis for allocating the number of members to each province was to be worked out. On April 21 of this year I placed on record in Hansard quotations from speeches by Sir Robert Borden, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, all agreeing in remarkably similar terms to the necessity for bringing the provinces into any discussion of such a change as is contemplated by the measure now before us.
I refer to Hansard of that date because I do not intend to read again quotations that are already on record during the course of the present session. The effect of these arguments can be summed up in the opening words of the speech I quoted of Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe on February 18, 1925, when he said:
I submit that this should be a matter for understanding between the dominion and the provinces, and it is a matter upon which, I am sure, agreement might and should be reached.

Without extending the quotation or the arguments, and in answer to the question asked by the Prime Minister, I would simply repeat what was said by Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe 27 years ago, that it is a subject upon which I am sure agreement might and should be reached. Unless agreement can be reached then we must immediately recognize that there are differences of opinion with respect to this matter which should be borne in mind at a time such a change is contemplated. I hope any argument that may be made in support of the adoption of this measure now before us will not seek to divert attention from the vitally important principle involved by arguing that no great harm is going to be produced as a result of what is now proposed.
If the original understanding which was the basis upon which confederation became possible is to be changed in this way without consultation with the provinces, then that principle may be extended right down the line. There is no doubt about the fact that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, Sir Robert Borden, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen and others on both sides of the house thought this was one of those agreements embedded in the constitution which could not be changed without consultation and understanding between the dominion government and the provinces.
It is true that we must be ready to keep pace in our thinking, our conduct, our legislative enactments and administrative procedures with the rapidly changing world in which we are now living and the rapid expansion of this country. There are some things, however, which do not change and Which are not related to the changing events, except in so far as there must be adjustments related to population. When the fathers of confederation agreed to the terms of the British North America Act, which became our basic constitution in 1867, they recognized in the terms of that constitution the fact that there were going to be changes in population They recognized that there were likely to be changes in the relationship of populations and the proportionate basis between the provinces. For that very reason they adopted a method of arithmetical computation which persisted through the long years until the amendments which have been referred to in the earlier discussion this afternoon.
The fact that an unsatisfactory method was adopted by this government on an earlier ion should not be accepted as an answer to any argument as to the impropriety of the course that is now being pursued. What it does do is emphasize the danger of a precedent; and to any hon. member who believes in the sanctity of the British North
British North America Act America Act I suggest that he recognize the extent to which this government is inclined to use a precedent established on one occasion as a justification for extending that precedent on some future occasion. The procedure now followed, under which the original understanding is abandoned, is one which is being employed on this particular occasion for the purpose of meeting a situation which most hon. members think should be met in some way. This is not the first time there has been a departure from the absolute arithmetical computation originally contemplated by the British North America Act.
I would recall the words of the minister who is moving that this measure be given second reading. This afternoon he told us that this is an historic moment. He told us that this is an occasion to remember, because we are now going to amend our own constitution without reference to Westminster. I hope hon. members will recall that we have supported the principle that Canadians should interpret their own constitution. Nevertheless, we have said that as we assume the authority and responsibility for amending our own constitution in Canada, we must be very careful not to depart from those basic principles which were accepted as part of the compact at the time the provinces joined to make one nation. We cannot measure the dangers that may lie in a denial of those basic principles, and in a refusal to consult the provinces, by any argument that may take place as to the absence of any danger in the actual results that will flow from the abandonment of that practice on this particular occasion.
I suggest now, Mr. Speaker, that since this is an historic moment; since this is the first occasion upon which the parliament of Canada is assuming full responsibility for amending its constitution in a matter of this kind, we should recognize the position of the provinces and seek their opinions before such an important step is taken. I find it very difficult to understand how anyone could seriously argue that the provinces are not interested in the results of this action. The very fact that we do not simply take some figure and use that to determine the number of seats throughout the whole of Canada, but that we use a formula for arriving at the number of seats in each province, and under the formula now adopted divide the population of the province by that figure to arrive at the number of seats in that province, recognizes that there is a provincial interest in the representation in this house. It recognizes that the representation of federal members is part and parcel of our federal system,

British North America Act and that the representation of a certain number of members from each province goes hand in hand with the whole system which was adopted under the act of confederation.
We have put this argument forward with the utmost earnestness, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that as we now proceed to amend our own constitution we will, at the very outset, recognize the rights of the provinces. I would ask hon. members who are considering the amendment now before them to examine what has been said in the past; to remember that no changing events have changed that basic principle, and that in this federal system we must not be at any time beguiled into accepting the arguments that would apply to a unitary state and which are certainly not applicable to a federation such as ours. The provinces have their place, just as the dominion has its place, and this amendment now before the house is simply intended to establish a recognition of that relationship between the provinces and the dominion which was clearly recognized at all times in the past, until by a somewhat uncertain route we arrived at a procedure which is not supported by those who were closer to the event and clearly understood what had guided those who so wisely laid the foundation of Canadian unity.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO READJUST REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I need detain the house long on this amendment, nor on the principle involved in the bill which is now under consideration. This debate is largely a repetition and perhaps

some development of the debates we had in this house in 1943, in 1946 and again in 1949; but I think it has been quite useful to have it today because it has brought about some degree of clarification of the differences between the parties on this matter concerning amendments to the Canadian constitution. Nevertheless I am somewhat puzzled to know just exactly what is intended by this amendment, which provides that consideration of the bill before the house be deferred until the principle thereof has been made the subject matter of consultation between the dominion and the provinces.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) stated that there were some matters that were so fundamental to the constitution that they should not be dealt with until there had been the agreement of all the provinces but that there might be others where the situation would be different if there were one or more dissenting provinces. I do not know just how that would apply to the provisions of this bill, but I will admit that it is difficult to make in advance definite pronouncements as to what would or should be done in circumstances of which the whole atmosphere is yet unknown.
I think I should endeavour to add something by way of clarifying the position I have constantly taken on this extremely important matter; and at the outset I wish to say that it is not a position taken since I have come into politics. These are the beliefs I have always held as a lawyer. In order to substantiate or to verify that statement, one would only have to refer to a speech I made as president of the Canadian Bar Association in 1931; it is contained in the proceedings of the Canadian Bar Association, volume 16, 1931, at pages 97 and following. There it will be found that my views at that time were that the British North America Act had distributed legislative and executive power between the federal authority on the one hand and the provincial authorities on the other hand; that while the situation remained as it was in 1867-that is to say, that the powers exercised in Canada were controlled by and subject to those of the parliament at Westminster-it might well be that the parliament at Westminster could and would modify the distribution that had been made in 1867, but that since the declaration of 1926 with regard to the equality of status of the various members of the commonwealth I did not believe that the parliament at Westminster would attempt to do anything to operate in Canada except at the request of the Canadian people made through their proper representatives.

That is the position I have always taken. I have always asserted that the terms of the B.N.A. Act were not the terms of a contract between the provinces because when the conferences were held prior to confederation there was one province of Canada, comprising Upper Canada and Lower Canada, there were no provinces of Ontario and Quebec; and there were the maritime provinces. At that time there was a compact between the representatives not merely of the people segregated by provincial boundaries; there was a compact between those who spoke for the two great principal races inhabiting these territories at that time. By referring to the speeches of Mr. Meighen, hon. gentlemen will find that was also his view, namely that it was not a compact between provinces-they did not exist-but that it was a compact between a majority and a minority as to the arrangement they were going to ask the parliament at Westminster to enact as statute law in what was to be the constitution of Canada. That is the way it was dealt with.
There was a conference at Charlottetown and there was a conference at Quebec. Then there was a conference in the Westminster hotel in London. There were successive drafts of the legislation which it was desired to put before the parliament at Westminster. The final form is, in substance, in accord with what had been accepted at the conference at Quebec, but in detail it is quite different from what had been the language used in the Quebec resolutions.
My view was and is that the legislative and executive jurisdiction given to one authority could not be taken from that authority without its consent, and that anything that would take from the provincial legislatures that part of the sovereignty of the Canadian people that was assigned to them, in accord with the compact by the B.N.A. Act, could not be taken from them without their express consent. But it must not be forgotten that the people of the provinces are also the people of Canada, and that that part of their sovereignty which was not entrusted to the local legislatures was entrusted to the general legislature. It is just as important to respect and preserve the rights, privileges and autonomy of the federal legislature as it is to be respectful of the rights and privileges of the local legislatures. It so happens that it is at this time our responsibility on what I may call the treasury benches to see to it that there is no abandonment by us of the rights and privileges given, in that distribution, to the federal authority.
British North America Act
With respect to representation in this house, in the Quebec resolutions it had been provided that the adjustment of constituencies in the provinces and of their boundaries would be something dealt with by the provincial legislatures. The general principle agreed upon was that the basis of representation in the House of Commons should be by population as determined by the official census every ten years. To work that out certain rules were established, and it was provided in resolution 19 that immediately after the completion of the census of 1871 and immediately after every decennial census thereafter the representation from each section in the House of Commons should be readjusted on the basis of population.
For the purposes of readjustment Lower Canada was to be assigned 65 seats; and its population was to be divided by 65, and the quotient was to determine the unit of representation in the other provinces. But there was also as a part of the agreement that the representation was to be on the basis of population, a qualification that would avoid too sudden changes. No province was to see its representation diminished if its proportion of the population had not decreased by as much as 5 per cent. It was then further provided in resolution 24 as follows:
The local legislature of each province may from time to time alter the electoral districts for the purposes of representation in the House of Commons, and distribute the representatives to which the province is entitled in any manner such legislature may think fit.
Well, that was in the Quebec resolutions. When these resolutions came before the legislature of the united Canadas, Sir John A. Macdonald presented an address to be submitted to Her Majesty for the adoption of a bill by the parliament of Westminster and the terms of paragraph 24 were changed in the address to read as follows:
The local legislature of each province may, from time to time, alter the electoral districts for the purposes of representation in such local legislature, and distribute the representatives to which the province is entitled in such local legislature, in any manner such legislature may see fit.
That gave rise to quite a debate, and in the course of that debate-I am reading now from page 39 of the confederation debates of 1865-Sir John A. Macdonald had this to say:
A good deal of misapprehension has arisen from the accidental omission of some words from the 24th resolution. It was thought that by it the local legislatures were to have the power of arranging hereafter, and from time to time of readjusting the different constituencies and settling the size and boundaries of the various electoral districts. The meaning of the resolution is simply this, that for the first general parliament, the arrangement of constituencies shall be made by the existing local legislatures; that in Canada, for instance, the present Canadian parliament shall arrange what are

British North America Act to be the constituencies of Upper Canada, and to make such changes as may be necessary in arranging for the seventeen additional members giyen to it by the constitution; and that it may also, if it sees fit, alter the boundaries of the existing constituencies of Lower Canada. In short, this parliament shall settle what shall be the different constituencies electing members to the first federal parliament. And so the other provinces, the legislatures of which will fix the limits of their several constituencies in the session in which they adopt the new constitution. Afterwards the local legislatures may alter their own electoral limits as they please, for their own local elections. But it would evidently be unproper to leave to the local legislature the power to alter the constituencies sending members to the general legislature after the general legislature shall have been called into existence. Were this the case, a member of the general legislature might at any time find himself ousted from his seat by an alteration of his constituency by the local legislature in his section. No, after the general parliament meets, in order that it may have full control of its own legislation, and be assured of its position, it must have the full power of arranging and rearranging the electoral limits of its constituencies as it pleases, such being one of the powers essentially necessary to such a legislature.
Well, the parliament of the united Canadas passed an address in the terms which I read to the house a moment ago giving the local legislatures the right to deal with their own local constituencies for the purposes of their own local legislatures. But apparently that did not completely settle the matter, because we find that in the resolutions adopted at the Westminster hotel when the delegates went over there to have the bill prepared and introduced, this section 24 was not expressly dealt with. There it was said that after each census the representation would be readjusted, but the resolution did not say by whom or how the readjustment would be made.

speechtext: That would be after each census?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO READJUST REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Yes. I find in Pope's confederation papers that the first draft that was prepared of the bill to be submitted to the parliament of Westminster contained as the twenty-fifth section the following:
On the completion of the official census of the population of the united colony in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and of each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time, as any act of the parliament of the united colony from time to time directs, according to the following rules: (Qu. the readjustment to be made by an independent authority, as some of the judges, to be specified in the imperial act.)
That matter was then apparently considered and discussed, and in the third draft that was dropped and the provision was couched in the language which we find originally adopted in the British North America Act of 1867 which provided that the readjustment would be made by parliament

or by such authority as was designated by parliament, and the opening lines of section 51 were:
On the completion ... of each decennial . . . census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time, as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides, subject and according to the following rules . . .
Then followed rules to carry out the basic principle of representation by population, with the qualification against too rapid or frequent changes. Well, it was the submission of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that this was a declaration that this was a matter within the jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament, and I think that is clearly the case. It is something which was placed within the jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament because, among other reasons, in the opinion of Sir John A. Macdonald it was essential that that be done and, to paraphrase his language, it would be improper to have it otherwise.
That being the case, it has always been my view that it was something-I will not say of no interest to the provinces if by "provinces" we mean the people who live within the boundaries of the provinces-but it is something which is not within the purview of those who represent that population in the provincial legislatures and in the provincial governments. It is something within the purview of those who represent that population in the federal parliament, here in this House of Commons.
It was for that reason that, in 1946 and in 1949, we on this side of the house resisted the suggestion that there should not be anything done about such matters without consulting the provinces, because in our view to consult the provinces would imply the recognition that it should not be done without their consent. If consultation does not mean that we are going to be guided and even bound by the results of consultation, then it is an empty form and something which should not be resorted to. And we here on this side of the house feel that it would be a betrayal of our duties to the people of Canada at large to abandon such responsibility to those who represent the population in the local legislatures of the respective provinces.
We think it is the right of the people of Canada generally to choose their representatives to speak for them in this general parliament on all matters which, in the distribution of legislative and executive powers, were assigned to the general parliament.
That does not mean we would not like to get agreement with the provincial governments with respect to an over-all formula to have all amendments to our constitution

within the power of the people of Canada by their elected representatives somewhere. And in order to attempt to bring that about we have a conference that is still in existence trying to work out a formula. When that conference met objections were made to the fact that we had taken, or we had asked and had obtained from the parliament at Westminster, the right to have, with respect to federal matters, the same jurisdiction the legislatures had with respect to provincial matters.
They said, "You should not have done that in advance when we were going to have this conference." Our reply was:	I think if
we can hit upon a general formula we will not object to discussing the possibility of compromise on that score, as upon everything else; and we will consider anything you may wish to suggest and about which you think the representatives in the legislatures or in the provincial governments should have something to say. We will consider it; but we do not undertake necessarily to do it, because we have as great responsibility to the general public of Canada as you have to the public of your own provinces.
There was some reference to section 51. Our position was that that was something that was not of particular concern to them. But we said, let us not break up on any of these matters until we see how far we can get general agreement, and just how much we are apart.
All these conferences, if they are to be successful, have to be ended with some degree of compromise on both sides. We were not in a position where we could give away the rights of the federal parliament; but we were in a position where we could discuss them, and where we could get to proposals that could not be binding upon the Canadian public until they had the approval of this parliament itself. We are still endeavouring to get agreement on the whole matter of the Canadian constitution. But, pending that, we think we did accomplish a useful step in the assertion of our national status in getting from the parliament at Westminster the right to do ourselves, right here in Ottawa, the things that we used to ask them to do and which they invariably did, when we asked them to do them.
We would not ask them, without the consent of the provinces, to vary or alter this distribution in legislative, administrative and executive jurisdiction. That was a fundamental basis of the compact between the two great races in 1867. But if we or some other parliament took the responsibility of doing it-well, since the Statute of Westminster I do not know just what would happen 55704-200
British North America Act there at Westminster. They have never yet refused to accede to a joint address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada; and they certainly would be in a very embarrassing position if any address went from the Senate and House of Commons of Canada asking them to do something which did disturb this distribution.
That is a hypothetical question, because I have every confidence in my fellow Canadians, enough confidence in them to believe that long after I cease to be in this house there will always be a majority here who will be respectful of what was the real basis of that compact between the two great races in 1867.
I do not wish to cite from my own speeches, but some hon. members will recall that when the late lamented and beloved member for Calgary West asked me if, according to that doctrine of mine, the parliament at Westminster could and would be apt to act upon a joint address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada to do away with the right of my people to speak the French language in this House of Commons, I had to reply that technically and legally I thought that that was the case. But I reminded the hon. member of the answer Felix made when he was being asked to dispose of St. Paul. He said that it was not the custom of the Romans to condemn a man without hearing him first. And it is not the custom of Canadians to go back on what they look upon as the moral undertakings of their ancestors toward each other in this confederation pact.
There is just one other point I wish to make. Thus far I have been speaking about this amendment. With respect to it I invite those who have any confidence in us to follow us and to vote it down. But as to the merits of the amendment proposed in the bill itself, I repeat what I said when I moved the resolution to refer the matter to the committee. I am going to support this bill. But it is a free vote. It is the responsibility of each and every one to decide for himself, having in mind the responsibility he feels to his constituency and to his country at large, whether or not the rules presently in section 51 should be modified or expanded.
I think it would be unfortunate to have those rules applied in all their rigour to a province which would thus see its representation cut down by 25 per cent. I think it would be a mistake to do that. Others may have other views about it. Others may feel that we all should abide by the rules of the game as they now stand. But, on the merits of the bill, and on deciding as to whether or

British North America Act not it should get second reading, I am going to vote that it should get second reading. But I state here and now that I will not regard as going back on me anyone of any party who feels that is not the right thing to do, and who votes against the second reading of the bill which would, of course, impose that rigid application of the rules of section 51 as they were adopted in 1946.
I have no doubt that my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris), who is sponsoring the bill, is going to vote for the bill he sponsored, but I have not asked any other of my colleagues what attitude he would take, nor have I asked any of those who make up the usual following of the government in this house what attitude they will take on the merits of the bill. I am not going to try to influence them in their attitude beyond letting them know what my own is going to be.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the question is put on the main motion there is another aspect of the matter of redistribution which we feel the house should consider. I have already indicated that it was my intention on behalf of this group to move a further amendment. Indeed, the amendment is one which I sought to move in the special committee on redistribution. It was ruled out .of order in that committee on the ground that the terms of reference given to the committee did not empower it to deal with the question of whether or not redistribution should be effected by an independent redistribution commission rather than by a committee of the House of Commons.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the subject of my amendment, and I shall move it in a form which, if adopted, would give to that committee the power to consider that very question. I thought the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) tonight anticipated that I might be raising this question when in discussing the amendment then before the house he referred to the fact that as long ago as 1867 at the Westminster hotel in London the question was raised as to whether the redistribution of

seats in the federal parliament should be carried out by a committee of parliament or whether it should be referred to some independent tribunal. Apparently the fathers of confederation and those who were associated with them did not see fit to determine at that time that it should be done that way, although in the wording of section 51 they left the door open by leaving it for parliament to decide what authority should carry out redistribution.
This question as to whether or not redistribution should be effected by an independent body rather than by parliament has come in for considerable attention in the last two decades. As the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has pointed out, just at the outbreak of world war II a bill had been prepared which he, in the name of the government, would have introduced but for the outbreak of the war. In other words, but for that tragic event we might already have had redistribution effected by an independent commission instead of by a committee of parliament. The matter was discussed again at the time of the last redistribution, namely in 1947. On that occasion I had the privilege on behalf of this group of moving an amendment to second reading of the representation bill suggesting that, as an alternative, the redistribution of that year should be referred to an independent commission.
I well remember the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec South on that occasion. He indicated his support of the principle of my amendment, and he reminded us of the bill he had prepared some years before. He said, however, that it was difficult and impractical in his view to set up an independent redistribution commission when redistribution was right at our doorstep. In other words his proposal was that we should deal with this matter some years in advance. Again in this session the hon. member for Quebec South brought this matter to the attention of this house and of the country in a very forceful manner in a speech he made on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. He has a bill on the order paper that would establish an independent redistribution commission; but he has counselled us-and mind you, his counsel must be taken into account-to the effect that it may be that we have to look ahead; it may be that when we are right at the problem of redistribution it is too late to change the method of that immediate redistribution. It may be that, as the hon. member for Quebec South says, we shall have to plan while we are in the very midst of one redistribution for a different method of dealing with the next and future redistributions.

In other words, the amendment I shall move carries out the spirit of that suggestion which was made earlier this session by the hon. member. May I remind hon. members that others have indicated their support for the principle of redistribution being undertaken by an independent body. I refer in particular to the view expressed by the late prime minister, Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. On February 3, 1947, when he spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, he answered a question which had been put to him by the then leader of the opposition, Mr. John Bracken. Mr. Bracken had expressed the hope that redistribution might be carried out by an independent commission. Mr. King's reply, which can be found on pages 67 and 68 of Hansard for that date, was that on several occasions he had expressed the personal view that redistribution should be carried out by an independent tribunal. He said that he still held that view, but he said, and I quote from Hansard:
I do not believe that the majority of hon. members take that view, and in that particular I am prepared to accept the will of the majority. I hope, however, that the day will come when the House of Commons of Canada will see the wisdom of allowing its redistribution to be made by some impartial tribunal and not by the members of the house themselves dealing with the matter in committee as in former years it has been dealt with.
I am not so sure that Mr. King was right that it was the view of the majority of the house that this way should not be tried, but at any rate that was the opinion expressed. Nevertheless, at the same time he expressed his personal opinion, and it was one that he had held for some time, that it should be done by an independent body.
Those of us who have spoken on this subject from time to time have quoted such authorities as Professor Norman Ward of the university of Saskatchewan. The hon. member for Quebec South quoted him when he spoke earlier this session, and so have some of the members in this group. I need not take the time to put some of the excellent quotations from Professor Ward on the record again, but I shall refer to a quotation that was put on Hansard on April 21, 1952, at page 1441, in which Professor Ward demonstrated clearly that this is an outmoded way of dealing with redistribution-that is, referring it to a committee of the House of Commons. He supports most strongly the suggestion of the hon. member for Quebec South that the time has come to refer the matter to an independent tribunal.
I remind hon. members as well of the tremendous interest there is in this question on the part of those who write the editorials in most of the newspapers of this country.

British North America Act It has been discussed this year in particular because redistribution is with us at the present time, and it is a subject of great interest. I think it is fair to say that the consensus of editorial writers in this country is that we should find a better way than by referring the question to a committee of this house; that we should set up machinery to make it possible for the problem to be handled by an independent commission. Hon. members are aware that the practice of referring the matter to an independent commission is followed in the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Australia, as well as other democratic countries. Indeed we are about the only democracy that still adheres to this outworn method of dealing with this problem.

speechtext:
I cannot say whether I have seen any editorial comments suggesting that this matter be settled by means of a constitutional amendment, but I am making that proposal, in line with what has been suggested by the hon. member for Quebec South, that we make a firm decision. What annoys me is that at redistribution time we can all agree that next time we should do it the other way, but then we let the years roll by and when the next time comes the same sentiments are expressed again, that we shall have to leave it over until the next time. It was for that reason I felt we should settle the question by writing into our constitution the necessary amendment. That it could be written in I think is borne out by the statement of the Prime Minister tonight to the effect that this was discussed at the Hotel Westminster in London back in 1867, and that is the suggestion I shall be making in the amendment I shall move in a few minutes.
May I also cite as support for our contention that redistribution should be carried out by an independent commission rather than by a committee of parliament the experience we are having right at this very time in dealing with redistribution. Professor Norman Ward, in the quotation I referred to a moment ago, said that, with the best will in the world, a group of M.P.'s drawn from many occupations, provinces and political parties would find it extremely difficult

to face objectively the various problems connected with this whole question of redistribution.
I think it is fair to say that we in this parliament think we are members with the best will in the world. Yet it is an understatement to suggest that we are having great difficulty in sorting out the problems associated with redistribution. Indeed, there are many knotty problems to be dealt with in that sphere before this session ends. In my view the experience hon. members are having right now should convince all the members of this house that the time has come to make a firm decision with regard to this matter.
The last time redistribution was up for consideration, namely in 1947, we moved an amendment to the motion for second reading of the representation bill the effect of which would have been to refer the redistribution of 1947 to an independent commission. That amendment was defeated. In my view such a move would be a valid one to make on this occasion. But there are those who might say that if one now tried to refer the present redistribution to an independent commission, that would result in delay, in fact in so much delay that the next election might have to be fought on the present boundaries. In my view that is not a sufficient argument against referring the matter to an independent commission for this very redistribution. However, I recognize the fact that if we were to move an amendment of that kind it would be beaten and no gain would be made.
Believing that it is our job to look to the future, Mr. Speaker, we are therefore going to propose instead that, in the light of our present experience, in the light of the opinions of people across this country and in the light of the advice of the hon. member for Quebec South, we now make a decision that this is the last time redistribution will be carried out by a committee of this house. We are going to propose that we now make the decision that, in the case of the redistribution to be effected after the decennial census of 1961 and every census thereafter, redistribution will be carried out by an independent commission to be established by parliament.
There will be much to do before 1961. A bill establishing such a commission will have to be prepared. That bill will have to specify the rules on the basis of which that commission will function. That bill will have to determine the composition of that commission, and to make certain of its independence. That bill would have to provide what would happen when the commission had finished its work and had reported its findings to Mr. JUNE 12, 1952
Speaker, for in the end the responsibility in connection with this matter would still rest with parliament.
The hon. member for Quebec South, in his bill, proposes a way of dealing with that problem. I am not going to comment as to whether his method is the best one or not; and he will agree with me that at this point that is not something for us to decide. The fact that he has worked it out in his bill is evidence of the fact that it can be done. My suggestion is that at this moment we should at least take the position that next time, and every time thereafter, redistribution is going to be carried out by an independent commission.
The way we propose that this matter should be dealt with, Mr. Speaker, is by referring the subject matter of the bill now before us to the special committee on redistribution which is still in existence and is still carrying on its work. In fact, procedurally we are rather fortunate that that committee is still meeting, because it makes it possible for us to deal with this matter in a manner which will not kill the effort now being made to amend the British North America Act in respect of the 15 per cent floor and in respect of two seats for Yukon and Mackenzie River. Our proposal is that the subject matter of this bill should be referred to the special committee on redistribution and that it should be given by this house power to do something which thus far it has not had the power to do, namely the power to consider whether the British North America Act should be amended to provide that the readjustment in the representation in the House of Commons to be effected following the decennial census of 1961, and following each decennial census thereafter, shall be made, subject to any rules to be prescribed by parliament, by an independent commission to be appointed by parliament for that purpose.
If the motion in those terms which I shall presently move were to pass the house tonight, that would mean that this house would express its support of the principle that we should have an independent commission after the next census, and it would also refer that matter to the committee to consider. The committee could then consider it and if it approved of the idea of amending the British North America Act in that respect it could present to the House of Commons a further report including a draft bill which would be the same as the draft bill it has already agreed upon plus the amendment that would be necessary to carry out the proposal I am presenting to the house tonight. In fact the amendment which was ruled out of order the other day, and which I moved
British North America Act in that committee, was designed to do that very thing; and I am satisfied that it would have done it. The only difficulty was that the chairman felt the committee did not have power, under its terms of reference, to deal with this phase of the matter. This house has the right to give that committee the power to deal with this phase of the matter and that is what we are asking for at this time.
I hope hon. members of the house will give serious consideration to this matter. Let us not put it off from one decade to another. Let us not, every time it comes up for consideration, agree amongst ourselves-privately, and in some instances publicly-that this is the wrong way to do it and that next time we must do it the other way, but do nothing about it. The result is that when the next time comes around and some member rises in the house and wants to refer the matter to an independent commission, there will be some other member from Quebec South here saying, "I agree with the idea but it is too late; redistribution is on our doorstep".
We have a duty to perform, particularly because of the experience we are having in dealing with this matter at the present time. I urge the house to give most serious consideration to the amendment which I shall now propose. I therefore move, seconded by my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis):
That Bill 331 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the special committee on redistribution with instructions that they have power to consider whether the British North America Act should be amended so as to provide that the readjustment in the representation in the House of Commons to be effected following the decennial census of 1961, and each decennial census thereafter, shall be made, subject to any rules to be prescribed by parliament, by an independent commission to be established by parliament for that purpose.

speechtext:
The question which the
Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has raised is an important one. He referred to standing order 60, which reads:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
The British North America Act provides that all legislation involving the expenditure of money must be recommended for the consideration of the house by His Excellency the Governor General. In dealing with the present amendment I am faced with the problem of determining whether it would involve the expenditure of money if carried. The Prime Minister has raised the question whether the word "house" includes select committees. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) has said that if a recommendation by the committee would necessarily involve the expenditure of money it would be out of order, and with that I agree. But would a mere recommendation of a committee necessarily involve an expenditure?
Let us suppose that this amendment carries. The question would then be considered

by the committee as to whether an independent commission should be set up. If that independent commission were set up it would clearly involve the expenditure of money. However, does the committee set up the commission? Clearly the committee could not set up the commission. Could the committee do more than bring in a report recommending that such commission be set up? Supposing the committee did make that recommendation would the house or the government be required to act upon it. In other words would the committee's report be a direction to the government to bring in legislation involving the expenditure of money?
This is an important question and I would not like a ruling given today on such limited reflection to be considered as binding on future occasions. There is some doubt in my mind as to whether it would be a direct order to the government to bring in such legislation. The government and the house I believe could reject the recommendation of the committee. As there is some doubt in my mind- and' I repeat that I do not want this ruling to be considered a binding precedent-I feel that I should allow the amendment to stand.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, though I am only too glad to support the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in his suggestion that his amendment is in order, that does not by any means imply that I believe the amendment to be a valid and proper one in the circumstances and on its merits. May I say at once that with respect to the bill I am by no means convinced that it should pass on its merits. I am quite satisfied with the amendment to the British North America Act which was made in 1946 and I see no great necessity for the amendment now proposed.
However, with respect to the amendment moved by my hon. friend and the complimentary references he made to my efforts to have a study made to bring about a scheme or plan whereby redistribution would be made by persons outside this House of Commons, I want to say here and now that although on two occasions I have presented a bill which would have had the effect of setting up some sort of commission to prepare a general plan of redistribution it was never my intention, and it is not my intention, that that should form part of our fundamental constitution.
I believe we have reached such a stage of confusion, are in such a practical morass, have got ourselves into such a mess with respect to redistribution by amending and modifying and changing the various principles with respect to representation by population, 55704-201
British North America Act with respect to geographic units, with respect to county boundaries that we must have a new deal. I have too much respect for the members of this house to burden them with the duty and responsibility of making that kind of new deal in connection with redistribution. However, I do not want to see us get away from the responsibility of parliament to carry out the duties which we as members have been sent here to do, the duty laid upon us by the British North America Act which says that redistribution shall be made by the parliament of Canada.
In the bill which I presented there _ is scarcely one section which would not require modification. I insist only on certain principles, namely, first, that we should start afresh; second, that parliament maintain its control and responsibility over the action it takes with respect to redistribution and, third, that we lay down some set of rules and regulations upon which we can base future redistributions.
With respect to some of the provisions of the bill it is quite clear to me, as it would be to anyone, that the position and status of the unfortunate civil servant whom I have nominated to be a sort of umpire between the upper millstone of Toryism and the lower millstone of Liberalism would be most unhappy. He would either be obliged to resign before the job was done or he would be fired by one or other of the parties when the job was completed. Therefore there should be at least some discussion on that section of the bill.
There are some sections which I think need to be carefully studied. There is above all a need for a brand new redistribution. The reason I think it should be taken out of the responsibility of members of the house is that it would place too heavy a burden on them. If the job were properly done it is extremely unlikely that any hon. member would be representing the same geographic unit after the job was over. I do not think members should be called upon to commit hara-kiri any more than they should be called upon to meet the importunities and pressures that would be brought upon them by local interests, by people attached to the traditions of the county and by people attached to party tradition. It is for that reason I suggest that for once anyway we ask people from outside the House of Commons to do the job. Where they will come from I am not prepared to say. Whether they are to be appointed, as I suggest in the bill, in a bi-partisan way or whether they are to be appointed in a non-partisan way makes no difference, but I do suggest that when they have made their report and have laid before parliament

British North America Act a plan and scheme for redistribution, parliament in the last analysis should be the judge whether that plan and scheme is or is not a proper one.
I am convinced, and it may be only a faint hope, that if some such redistribution is made then notwithstanding local objections, notwithstanding the difficulties and the obstacles which will confront individual members of parliament, a plan of that kind presented to the people of Canada would carry such force and authority that it would be very difficult to alter or modify it in any degree.
With respect to the specific amendment of my hon. friend, I do not think he would expect me to support it. I have been too outspoken in my objection to commissions, bureaux and bureaucrats receiving delegated powers to do jobs which should be done by this assembly, this House of Commons, to now be willing to enshrine in the ark of the covenant of our constitution an omnipotent bureaucracy to do the work of redistribution which is primarily our concern. I have no objection to creating non-partisan machinery to do the job in order to give us a pattern of what we should do for the future, but I do not think we should place in the constitution of this country for all time and, as my hon. friend further says, for the next census and for the censuses to come, any provision which will free us from the responsibility which has been laid upon us.
Again with respect to this particular amendment, my hon. friend does not anticipate that it will be effective immediately. He says it needs to be effective only in the census of 1961. Why does he not join with me at the next session in an endeavour to prepare some kind of bill that will pass the house or at least be referred to a committee for discussion? With our joint efforts in the ten years to come we might achieve something. As it is now all he would get from the committee- and I would be glad to get it too, but not in the form of a constitutional amendment- would be a sort of pious hope that some day we would have a commission. I suggest that the two of us get together, hammer out a bill, endeavour to overcome the obstacle of its being out of order, and eventually convince our colleagues that that is the proper thing to do for at least once.
